Framework Reference

What can be checked, and how

Evidence

By Dale Edward · Corrections and challenges: open an issue on GitHub

These pages ask readers to act on them with their own money, so they should show their work. Two gaps come first. The dashboard’s code is private, so the formulas these pages describe cannot yet be checked against the software that runs them. And nothing here has a track record: the rules were designed, not fitted, and they have not been tested against a benchmark or run with real money in public. This page sorts the main claims by the kind of evidence behind them, says where each can be checked, lists what cannot be checked yet, and keeps a dated record of every correction and every decision.

The claims The limits The record Corrections Open arithmetic Part 1’s tests The review questions

The Limits

What we cannot show yet.

The dashboard’s code is private. The Math page transcribes the formulas the dashboard runs, but a reader cannot check that transcription against the code. Publishing the scoring module, or a public harness that reproduces the published examples from the same code, would close the gap.

Part of every score comes from the ticker symbol. As of October 2026, the dashboard adds a fixed offset, computed from each holding’s ticker symbol, at 41 places in its scoring code: up to 20 percent of a sub-score’s maximum, to keep scores from bunching at the same value. The offset carries no information about the asset. In our tests, holdings with identical data scored up to about 4.5 points apart on CIS and, with sparse data, up to about 35 points apart on a single component, for this reason alone. For individual stocks the offset on the convexity component only ever raises the score; for ETFs and crypto tokens it can move it either way. Because sizing uses bands, it matters most near a band’s edge, where it can move a holding into the next band.

Scores are structured judgment. Where reported data is missing, sub-scores use AI-generated estimates, at a discount, where they exist, and otherwise defaults set by posture and sector. The score is capped as usable coverage thins (AI estimates count toward it): at 75 below 70 percent coverage, 68 below 50 percent and 60 below 30 percent. The lowest cap still falls in the standard sizing band (60 to 69), so a holding with under 30 percent coverage can be sized as standard. A capped score means “not enough data,” not “average.”

No backtest and no track record. The rules were designed, not fitted to past returns, and they have not been tested against a benchmark or run with real money in public.

We grade our own tests. Part 1’s tests are scored by us. The data and the script are public so that anyone can rerun them and disagree.

No independent review yet. These pages are published under a pen name. The 2026 review was internal: an AI model checked the claims against primary sources, and the author decided each finding. The corrections below are what it found.

The Record

Every change, and every decision not to change.

This record logs, with date and reason: every change to a rule, weight or threshold published in these pages; every change to a named instrument; each February’s readings of Part 1’s tests; and every event that tests a named instrument’s qualifying criteria (a monthly price move of more than 20 percent; a missed, deferred or reduced distribution; a rating action; a lawsuit filed against the issuer). Each “no change” entry says what would have changed it. Entries dated before October 2026 were written after the fact, and say so. The record is kept in the public repository, where every change carries its date.

On June 29 Strategy raised the rate from 11.5 to 12 percent a year, paid semi-monthly from July 1.No change to STRC’s role as the framework’s named income Ballast.STRC qualifies as Ballast under the three-of-five rule on durable cash generation (for a preferred, its distribution record: paid in every period since issuance), low factor correlation (the monthly rate reset is designed to hold its price near its $100 stated amount) and a liquidity-resilient valuation (its $100 stated amount and rate-reset support). It carries no agency credit rating as a new instrument; the framework reads the issuer’s Bitcoin asset coverage as its measure of balance-sheet strength. What would change it: the commitment is to the slot, not the name. The case study holds its return-of-capital income and deployment sleeve at 12 percent under a documented override, reviewed at each quarterly Ballast reassessment and sooner on material deterioration; STRC holds the slot today. It would give up the slot if it stopped meeting three of the five Ballast criteria (a missed, deferred or reduced distribution would end the distribution record that counts as its cash generation), or if a stronger candidate for the slot appeared. Either change is logged here with its date.

Open Arithmetic

Rerun it yourself.

The documentation is public: github.com/Tataku/ACF-Docs. Clone it and run npm test. Among the suite’s checks, 20 recompute the worked examples from the inputs each page states: the headroom formula and its examples, the Bitcoin headroom and network-convexity examples, catalyst decay, the FIS floor and multiplier, the sizing bands, the size-opportunity curve, the FIS example book, Part 3’s case study, drawdowns, addressable-market and gold scenarios, reserve arithmetic and loan-to-value passage, Part 4’s Roth case and tax-wedge charts, Part 5’s wrapper compounding (1.1030 against 1.07530) and Part 2’s tax-drag multiples.

Another 7 recompute every figure Part 1 derives from committed public data (data/part1-history/, read by scripts/part1-history.mjs): the 60/40 and Treasury returns after inflation, the debt and interest checkpoints, the inflation figures, 2022’s rank since 1928, and the readings behind Part 1’s tests. Part 1’s Bitcoin, yield and sequence-of-returns figures are checked against their cited sources, not yet by a test.

The same suite confirms that each of the 46 charts declares its data mode and names its sources, and that a chart labeled as plotted data names each series, its range and its retrieval date. It does not compare a drawn line with its sources; the source links are there for that.

The Tests

Part 1’s tests: method and readings.

Read each February. Tests 2 and 4 run from the start of 2026; about nine months of that window had passed when they were set. 60/40 means 60 percent US stocks (S&P 500 with dividends) and 40 percent 10-year Treasuries, rebalanced each January; returns after inflation are compounded from Aswath Damodaran’s annual series (NYU Stern) and the December-to-December change in the BLS consumer price index. The readings below are computed from the committed data when this page is built.

The Review

The questions a model review asks.

US bank supervisors ask four questions of any model a bank relies on. They were set out in SR 11-7 (2011), which the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC replaced in April 2026 with SR 26-2, keeping them. That guidance is written for banks. We use its questions because they apply to any model people act on; we do not claim to meet it, and no regulator has reviewed these pages.

Where these pages stand on each question
QuestionWhere these pages answer itWhere we stand
Conceptual soundness: is the design sound, and are its assumptions stated?The Parts state each rule and its reasoning; the Math page states the formulas; the scope notes state the assumptions.Partial: the formulas cannot be checked against the private code
Ongoing monitoring: is it still working as intended?The forward record, the February readings and the corrections.Starts with the first readings
Outcomes analysis: do its outputs match what happened?Not yet possible: no backtest and no real-money record.Open
Effective challenge: has someone objective and informed tried to break it?The 2026 review was internal. Corrections and challenges are invited as public GitHub issues.Open
